target_audience: University students with a basic interest in computer science and mathematics

outline.target_audience: University students with a basic interest in computer science and mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The One-Way Street (Hashing)
sections.content: Introduce cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256). Explain that they are 'one-way'—easy to compute forward, impossible to reverse. Visualize this as a 'digital fingerprint' generator.
sections.example: Imagine a blender: putting in a strawberry makes a unique smoothie, but you can never turn the smoothie back into a strawberry.

sections.title: The Digital Puzzle: Proof of Work
sections.content: Explain the mining process. Computers must find a 'nonce' that, when combined with transaction data, produces a hash starting with a specific number of zeros. This is a game of trial and error.
sections.example: A group of robots guessing a combination lock code. As the difficulty increases, the lock requires more digits to be correct, making it exponentially harder to guess.

sections.title: Chaining the Blocks
sections.content: Describe the blockchain data structure. Each block contains the hash of the *previous* block. This creates an unbreakable chronological link. If you change one transaction, the subsequent hashes become invalid.
sections.example: A series of glass boxes where each box contains a key to the next. If you break into the first box, the connection to all subsequent boxes snaps instantly, alerting everyone.

sections.title: Ownership: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
sections.content: Explain how private and public keys work. Based on the discrete logarithm problem, it is easy to derive a public key from a private key, but impossible to do the reverse.
sections.example: A magical 'stamp' (private key) that can only be used by its owner to sign a document, while the world uses a 'public sensor' to verify that the stamp belongs to you without ever seeing the stamp itself.

sections.title: Summary and Synthesis
sections.content: Connect these pieces: Hashing secures the data, Proof-of-Work prevents tampering, and Elliptic Curves provide identity. Together, they create a decentralized trust system.
sections.example: Visualize the entire network as a digital beehive where every bee (node) keeps a perfect record, and changing one cell requires the effort of the entire colony.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The One-Way Street (Hashing)
lecture_lines: Cryptographic hashes create unique digital fingerprints.
The process is strictly a one-way street.
Input data is transformed into a fixed digest.
Reversing the operation is mathematically impossible.
Think of it as a permanent blender effect.

storyboard.title: The Digital Puzzle: Proof of Work
lecture_lines: Proof of Work validates network activity.
Miners guess nonces for specific hash results.
This trial and error requires immense effort.
animations: Highlight #00FF00 valid hash starting with zeroes.

storyboard.title: Chaining the Blocks
lecture_lines: Blocks chain together via previous hashes.
This creates an immutable chronological history.
Altering one link invalidates the entire chain.
animations: Show Block A #FF0000 linking to Block B.
Draw #00FF00 pointer from Block B to Block A hash.

storyboard.title: Ownership: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
lecture_lines: Elliptic curve cryptography secures user ownership.
Private keys sign, public keys verify identity.
Deriving private keys is computationally infeasible.
animations: Show #FF0000 Private Key signing a transaction.
Show #00FF00 Public Key verifying the signature.

storyboard.title: Summary and Synthesis
lecture_lines: Hashing, Proof-of-Work, and ECC form Bitcoin.
These primitives enable decentralized trust systems.
The network acts as a global ledger.
